summary: This RFC specifies algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encoding for the stateful hash-based signature schemes HSS, XMSS, and XMSS^MT in X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists. These schemes rely on hash functions, which are considered strong against quantum computers.

eli5.summary: Some signing methods rely only on scrambling functions, which is a sturdy basis. This says how to name and write them down in digital ID cards.

questions: what is hss xmss in x.509
why can xmss keys not be reused
subtitle: How to name and encode HSS, XMSS and XMSS^MT hash-based signature keys in X.509 certificates and CRLs.

tldr.problem: Stateful hash-based signature schemes stay secure even when quantum computers become available, but X.509 certificates had no complete way to identify XMSS and XMSS^MT keys and signatures.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines object identifiers, absent parameters, OCTET STRING public key types, key usage rules and signature rules so HSS, XMSS and XMSS^MT can be used in certificates and CRLs.
tldr.outcome: The schemes have a hard limit: each private key can sign only a limited number of messages and its state must never be reused, so the RFC steers them to uses like firmware signing, software signing and CA certificates.

today: RFC 9802 was published in June 2025 as a Proposed Standard, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9708 for the HSS identifier.

sections.title: Stateful Hash-Based Signatures
sections.content:
The Hierarchical Signature System (HSS), the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS) and XMSS^MT combine Merkle trees with One-Time Signatures (OTS). They provide digital signatures that remain secure when quantum computers become available, and their security depends only on the underlying hash function.

The cost is state. A private key is a finite collection of OTS keys plus state that tracks their use. Only a limited number of messages can be signed, and the state must be updated and persisted after signing to prevent reuse of OTS keys. Parameters could allow a virtually unbounded number of signatures (for example 2^60), but at the cost of larger signatures and longer signing time. Because of this, the schemes may be unsuitable for interactive protocols.
sections.eli5: Think of a pad of one-time tickets. Each ticket can be used once, so you must always remember which ones you have already torn off.

sections.title: Where These Keys Fit
sections.content:
Because OTS signatures must never be reused, stateful schemes are inappropriate for general use. The conditions are left to certificate policies, with the guideline from NIST SP 800-208: they suit applications that need a signature scheme soon, will have a long lifetime and cannot practically switch to another scheme later.

The RFC names use cases where the signer can control the signing environment and the number of signatures is small and predictable: firmware signing, software signing and Certification Authority (CA) certificates. Stateful keys are generally not appropriate for end-entity certificates, although code signing is an exception where signing is often tightly controlled. Root CAs sign in a more secure environment and issue fewer certificates than subordinate CAs, so stateful keys fit root CA certificates better. A subordinate CA may qualify if it matches those restrictions, for example by issuing only code-signing certificates.
sections.eli5: A limited-use stamp is best kept in a locked room and used by a careful person, not handed to everyone.

sections.title: Algorithm and Public Key Identifiers
sections.content:
Each scheme has its own object identifier (OID) in the AlgorithmIdentifier, and the parameters field MUST be absent for all three.

  • HSS uses id-alg-hss-lms-hashsig, defined in RFC 9708 and repeated here. It is also called id-alg-mts-hashsig, a name from an early draft of RFC 8554.
  • XMSS uses id-alg-xmss-hashsig, arc 34 under the PKIX algorithms arc.
  • XMSS^MT uses id-alg-xmssmt-hashsig, arc 35.

The hash function and tree height are identified inside the public key and signature values, as defined by RFC 8554, RFC 8391 and SP 800-208. In a SubjectPublicKeyInfo the subjectPublicKey BIT STRING holds the public key encoding from those documents. The RFC also defines an OCTET STRING type for each key (such as HSS-LMS-HashSig-PublicKey) for use outside SubjectPublicKeyInfo. A single-tree LMS key is HSS with one level.
sections.eli5: Each kind of stamp gets its own name tag so anyone reading the card knows which kind it is.

sections.title: Key Usage Bits
sections.content:
The keyUsage extension of RFC 5280 says what a key is for. When one of these algorithms appears in the public key of a CA certificate, the extension MUST contain at least one of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign or cRLSign, and MUST NOT contain other values.

For an end entity certificate the allowed values are digitalSignature, nonRepudiation or cRLSign, again with no others.
sections.eli5: The card lists what the stamp may be used for, and anything not on the list is forbidden.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms and Key Generation
sections.content:
The same OIDs identify the signatures, and the encoding MUST omit the parameters field. The signature algorithm identifier is a SEQUENCE of one component. No digest is applied before signing: the full data to be signed is signed, not a digest of it.

Signature formats come from RFC 8554 (HSS) and Appendices B.2 and C.2 of RFC 8391 (XMSS and XMSS^MT). The octet string is placed directly in the BIT STRING without extra ASN.1 wrapping, which in certificates and CRLs is the signatureValue field. For XMSS and XMSS^MT, both signature generation and key generation MUST follow Section 7.2 of SP 800-208.
sections.eli5: The whole message is signed directly, not a short summary of it, and the signature is attached as is.

sections.title: State Management and Backup
sections.content:
The security requirements of SP 800-208 MUST be taken into account. If an attacker obtains signatures for two different messages made with the same OTS key, forgeries become computationally feasible, so extreme care is needed to avoid accidental reuse. A user must also know how many signatures they intend to make, or risk exhausting the OTS keys.

Strategies include logging OTS key indexes, possibly outside the signing device, and checking the log before releasing a signature; using the key for only a moderate number of signatures; and reserving upcoming states in advance, as in McGrew's state reservation approach.

Backup and restore need special care. Duplicating keys or running redundant signing devices, as one might with a stateless scheme such as SLH-DSA, will lead to OTS reuse with high probability. Safer strategies are in Section 7 of SP 800-208.
sections.eli5: Copying the pad of tickets to a second office is dangerous, because both offices might tear off the same ticket.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Examples
sections.content:
IANA registered module OID 114 (id-mod-pkix1-shbs-2024) in the SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier registry. In the SMI Security for PKIX Algorithms registry it registered 34 (id-alg-xmss-hashsig) and 35 (id-alg-xmssmt-hashsig).

The RFC also gives an ASN.1 module for reference, and appendices with example X.509 v3 certificates for HSS, XMSS and XMSS^MT.
sections.eli5: The new name tags were written into the official list so nobody else reuses them.
